about: Analysis I is a 24-lecture Lent Term course in Part IA of the Cambridge Mathematical Tripos. Following the official schedule it rebuilds calculus rigorously: limits and convergence of sequences and series, continuity, differentiability (including the mean value theorem and Taylor's theorem), complex power series and the exponential and trigonometric functions, and the Riemann integral. It is examined on Paper 1 together with Vectors and Matrices; each Part IA paper has a Section I of shorter questions and a Section II of longer ones. The schedule marks the direct proof that power series are differentiable as non-examinable.
topics: Differentiability and the mean value theorem
Power series and radius of convergence
The fundamental theorem of calculus and improper integrals

notes.body:
Analysis I is the Lent Term course in which calculus is rebuilt rigorously from the properties of the real numbers. Everything rests on the definition of a limit and on completeness.

Definition of convergence
A sequence (aₙ) of real or complex numbers converges to a if
for every ε > 0 there is N such that |aₙ − a| < ε for all n ≥ N.
Limits are unique. Convergent sequences are bounded.

Worked example
aₙ = (2n + 1)/(n + 3) → 2. Indeed |aₙ − 2| = |2n + 1 − 2n − 6|/(n + 3) = 5/(n + 3), which is < ε whenever n > 5/ε. So given ε, take N to be any integer greater than 5/ε.

Algebra of limits
If aₙ → a and bₙ → b then aₙ + bₙ → a + b, aₙbₙ → ab, and aₙ/bₙ → a/b provided b ≠ 0 (bₙ is then non-zero for large n). Each is proved from the definition; for products use |aₙbₙ − ab| ≤ |aₙ||bₙ − b| + |b||aₙ − a| and boundedness of (aₙ).

Completeness
The real numbers satisfy the least upper bound property: every non-empty set bounded above has a supremum. An equivalent form, often called the fundamental axiom of analysis, is:
- every increasing sequence that is bounded above converges (to its supremum).
This fails in ℚ: the decimal approximations 1, 1.4, 1.41, … to √2 are increasing and bounded but have no rational limit.

Standard limits
- 1/n → 0 (Archimedean property).
- xⁿ → 0 if |x| < 1.
- n^(1/n) → 1.
- nᵏxⁿ → 0 for |x| < 1 and any fixed k.

Subsequences and Bolzano–Weierstrass
Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem: every bounded sequence in ℝ has a convergent subsequence. Two standard proofs:
- Bisection: repeatedly halve an interval containing infinitely many terms and use the fundamental axiom on the endpoints.
- Monotone subsequence: every real sequence has a monotone subsequence (consider 'peak' terms that are at least as large as all later terms); a bounded monotone sequence converges.
In ℂ, apply the real theorem to real parts, then to imaginary parts of the resulting subsequence.

Cauchy sequences
(aₙ) is Cauchy if for every ε > 0 there is N with |aₘ − aₙ| < ε for all m, n ≥ N.
General principle of convergence: a sequence in ℝ or ℂ converges if and only if it is Cauchy.
Proof of the hard direction: a Cauchy sequence is bounded (take ε = 1); by Bolzano–Weierstrass a subsequence converges to some a; then, for large m and n with aₙ in the subsequence, |aₘ − a| ≤ |aₘ − aₙ| + |aₙ − a| is small.
The value of this criterion is that it proves convergence without knowing the limit, which is exactly what is needed for series.

Exam tips: Section I questions often ask for an ε–N proof from scratch. Write the definition, do the algebra to find a suitable N, and state the conclusion clearly. Never 'divide' by a limit without checking it is non-zero.

A series Σaₙ converges if its partial sums sₙ = a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ converge. The schedule asks for absolute convergence and the comparison, ratio and alternating series tests.

First facts
- If Σaₙ converges then aₙ → 0 (since aₙ = sₙ − sₙ₋₁). The converse is false.
- Geometric series: Σ xⁿ (n ≥ 0) converges if and only if |x| < 1, with sum 1/(1 − x).
- Harmonic series Σ 1/n diverges: grouping 1/2 + (1/3 + 1/4) + (1/5 + ⋯ + 1/8) + ⋯, each bracket is at least 1/2.
- Σ 1/n² converges: for n ≥ 2, 1/n² ≤ 1/(n(n − 1)) = 1/(n − 1) − 1/n, which telescopes.
- More generally Σ 1/nᵏ converges if and only if k > 1 (e.g. via the integral test, covered at the end of the course; neither it nor Cauchy condensation is named in the schedule, but both are standard).

Comparison test
If 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ for all n and Σbₙ converges, then Σaₙ converges (its partial sums are increasing and bounded above). Contrapositive: if Σaₙ diverges, so does Σbₙ.

Absolute convergence
Σaₙ converges absolutely if Σ|aₙ| converges. Absolute convergence implies convergence, for real or complex terms. Proof via Cauchy: |aₘ₊₁ + ⋯ + aₙ| ≤ |aₘ₊₁| + ⋯ + |aₙ|, so the partial sums of Σaₙ are Cauchy whenever those of Σ|aₙ| are. (For real terms you can also split into positive and negative parts.)

Ratio test
If aₙ ≠ 0 and |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| → l, then:
- l < 1: Σaₙ converges absolutely;
- l > 1: Σaₙ diverges (terms do not tend to 0);
- l = 1: no conclusion (Σ1/n diverges, Σ1/n² converges, both with l = 1).

Root test (a standard extra, not named in the schedule)
If |aₙ|^(1/n) → l, the same three conclusions hold.

Alternating series test
If (aₙ) is decreasing and aₙ → 0, then Σ(−1)^(n+1) aₙ converges. Proof idea: the even partial sums increase, the odd ones decrease, and they differ by a term tending to 0.

Conditional convergence
Σ(−1)^(n+1)/n converges (alternating series test) but not absolutely. Such series are delicate: rearranging their terms can change the sum (Riemann), whereas absolutely convergent series can be rearranged freely. (Rearrangements go beyond the schedule; treat this as background.)

Worked examples
- Σ n²/2ⁿ: ratio (n + 1)²/(2n²) → 1/2 < 1, so it converges.
- Σ n!/nⁿ: ratio (n + 1)! nⁿ/((n + 1)^(n+1) n!) = (n/(n + 1))ⁿ = (1 + 1/n)^(−n) → 1/e < 1, so it converges.
- Σ 1/(n² + n): compare with 1/n², or telescope 1/n − 1/(n + 1) to get sum 1.
- Σ sin(n)/n²: |sin n/n²| ≤ 1/n², so it converges absolutely.

Choosing a test
- Terms not tending to 0: diverges immediately.
- Factorials or nth powers: ratio or root test.
- Rational functions of n: compare with Σ1/nᵏ.
- Alternating signs with decreasing terms: alternating series test (then check absolute convergence separately).

Exam tips: state the test you use and check its hypotheses (non-negative terms for comparison; monotonic decrease for the alternating test). When the ratio test gives l = 1, say so and switch method.

Continuity is short in the schedule (three lectures) but supplies two theorems used constantly afterwards: the intermediate value theorem and the fact that a continuous function on a closed bounded interval is bounded and attains its bounds.

Definitions
Let f: E → ℂ with E ⊆ ℝ or ℂ, and a ∈ E. f is continuous at a if
for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |x − a| < δ, x ∈ E implies |f(x) − f(a)| < ε.
Equivalent sequential form: f is continuous at a if and only if f(xₙ) → f(a) for every sequence xₙ → a in E.
Similarly, lim_(x→a) f(x) = l means: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with 0 < |x − a| < δ (x ∈ E) implying |f(x) − l| < ε.

Building continuous functions
Sums, products, quotients (where the denominator is non-zero) and composites of continuous functions are continuous. So polynomials and rational functions are continuous where defined. The sequential form makes these proofs short, using the algebra of limits.

Examples and non-examples
- f(x) = x sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0, f(0) = 0, is continuous at 0, since |f(x)| ≤ |x|.
- sin(1/x) cannot be made continuous at 0: along xₙ = 1/(nπ) it is 0, along xₙ = 1/(2nπ + π/2) it is 1.
- The indicator function of ℚ is discontinuous everywhere (every interval contains rationals and irrationals).

The intermediate value theorem
If f: [a, b] → ℝ is continuous and f(a) < η < f(b), then f(c) = η for some c ∈ (a, b).
Proof sketch: let S = {x ∈ [a, b] : f(x) < η}. S is non-empty (a ∈ S) and bounded, so c = sup S exists. If f(c) < η, continuity gives points slightly to the right of c in S, contradicting c = sup S. If f(c) > η, continuity gives an interval to the left of c outside S, so a smaller upper bound exists, contradicting that c is the least upper bound. So f(c) = η.
Applications:
- Every positive real has an nth root (apply to xⁿ on [0, max(1, y)]).
- Every real polynomial of odd degree has a real root.
- A continuous f: [0, 1] → [0, 1] has a fixed point (apply the IVT to f(x) − x).

Boundedness and attaining bounds
If f: [a, b] → ℝ is continuous then f is bounded, and there are points where f attains its supremum and its infimum.
Proof of boundedness: if not, pick xₙ with |f(xₙ)| > n. By Bolzano–Weierstrass a subsequence converges to some x ∈ [a, b] (the interval is closed). Continuity gives f(x_(nⱼ)) → f(x), contradicting unboundedness.
Proof of attainment: let M = sup f. If f never equals M, then g(x) = 1/(M − f(x)) is continuous and so bounded, by K say; but M − f(x) can be made arbitrarily small, so g is unbounded. Contradiction.

Why the hypotheses matter
- Open interval: f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1) is continuous but unbounded; f(x) = x on (0, 1) is bounded but never attains its supremum 1.
- Discontinuity: f(x) = x on [0, 1) with f(1) = 0 never reaches its supremum 1.

Exam tips: when proving the theorems, say exactly where you use completeness (supremum or Bolzano–Weierstrass) and closedness of [a, b] (the subsequence limit stays in the interval).

notes.h: Differentiability and the mean value theorem
notes.body:
This section proves the standard rules of differentiation and then the mean value theorem, which turns information about f′ into information about f.

Definition
f: E → ℝ (E ⊆ ℝ) is differentiable at x with derivative f′(x) if
lim_(h→0) (f(x + h) − f(x))/h = f′(x).
Equivalently f(x + h) = f(x) + hf′(x) + hε(h) where ε(h) → 0 as h → 0. This form makes proofs of the rules clean, and it shows immediately that differentiable implies continuous. The converse fails: |x| is continuous but not differentiable at 0 (the difference quotient is +1 from the right and −1 from the left).

Rules
- Sums, products: (fg)′ = f′g + fg′.
- Quotients: (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g² where g ≠ 0.
- Chain rule: (f ∘ g)′(x) = f′(g(x)) g′(x).
- Example: d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹ by induction using the product rule.

Rolle's theorem
If f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then f′(c) = 0 for some c ∈ (a, b).
Proof: f attains its maximum and minimum on [a, b]. If both occur at endpoints, f is constant and any c works. Otherwise there is an interior extremum c, and at an interior maximum the difference quotient is ≤ 0 from the right and ≥ 0 from the left, forcing f′(c) = 0.

Mean value theorem (MVT)
If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then f(b) − f(a) = f′(c)(b − a) for some c ∈ (a, b).
Proof: apply Rolle to g(x) = f(x) − kx, with k = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) chosen so that g(a) = g(b).

Consequences
- If f′ = 0 on an interval then f is constant.
- If f′ > 0 on an interval then f is strictly increasing.
- Inequalities: |sin x − sin y| ≤ |x − y|, since |cos| ≤ 1.
- Example: for x > 0, x/(1 + x) < log(1 + x) < x, by applying the MVT to log(1 + t) on [0, x], where the derivative 1/(1 + c) lies between 1/(1 + x) and 1.

Cauchy's mean value theorem (a standard extra, not named in the schedule)
If f, g are continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then for some c ∈ (a, b),
(f(b) − f(a)) g′(c) = (g(b) − g(a)) f′(c).
Proof: apply Rolle to h(x) = (f(b) − f(a))g(x) − (g(b) − g(a))f(x). This underlies Taylor's theorem and L'Hôpital-type arguments.

Inverse functions (one-dimensional inverse function theorem)
If f: [a, b] → ℝ is continuous, differentiable on (a, b) with f′(x) > 0 there, then f is strictly increasing, its inverse g: [f(a), f(b)] → [a, b] is continuous, and g is differentiable on (f(a), f(b)) with
g′(y) = 1/f′(g(y)).
Example: g(y) = y^(1/n) on (0, ∞) has g′(y) = 1/(n g(y)ⁿ⁻¹) = (1/n) y^(1/n − 1).

A useful example
f(x) = x² sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0, f(0) = 0, is differentiable everywhere with f′(0) = 0 (since |f(h)/h| ≤ |h|), but f′(x) = 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x) for x ≠ 0 has no limit as x → 0. So a derivative need not be continuous.

Exam tips: check all hypotheses when quoting Rolle or the MVT (continuity on the closed interval, differentiability on the open one). The auxiliary function is the key idea in every proof; learn them.

Taylor's theorem makes precise how well a polynomial approximates a smooth function, and the last part of the differentiability section extends the derivative to complex functions.

Taylor's theorem with Lagrange's remainder
Suppose f and its derivatives up to f^(n−1) are continuous on [a, a + h] and f^(n) exists on (a, a + h). Then
f(a + h) = f(a) + hf′(a) + (h²/2!)f″(a) + ⋯ + (h^(n−1)/(n − 1)!)f^(n−1)(a) + Rₙ,
where Rₙ = (hⁿ/n!) f^(n)(a + θh) for some θ ∈ (0, 1).
The case n = 1 is exactly the mean value theorem.

Idea of the proof
Define F(t) = f(a + t) minus its Taylor polynomial of degree n − 1 at a, minus a multiple Btⁿ chosen so that F(h) = 0. Then F(0) = F′(0) = ⋯ = F^(n−1)(0) = 0 and F(h) = 0. Applying Rolle's theorem repeatedly gives successive points where F′, F″, …, F^(n) vanish, and F^(n)(θh) = 0 for some θ ∈ (0, 1). Since F^(n)(t) = f^(n)(a + t) − n!B, this identifies B = f^(n)(a + θh)/n!.

Worked example
For sin with n = 5 at a = 0: the derivatives at 0 are 0, 1, 0, −1, 0, and the fifth derivative is cos. So
sin x = x − x³/6 + (x⁵/120) cos(θx),
and therefore |sin x − (x − x³/6)| ≤ |x|⁵/120. For x = 0.1 the cubic approximation is within about 8.3 × 10⁻⁸. (sin and cos are defined properly via power series later in the course.)

Local extrema
If f′(a) = 0 and f″ is continuous near a with f″(a) > 0, Taylor's theorem with n = 2 gives f(a + h) − f(a) = (h²/2)f″(a + θh) > 0 for small h ≠ 0, so a is a strict local minimum. The analogous statement with f″(a) < 0 gives a local maximum.

Taylor series need not converge to f
Even when f has derivatives of all orders, the remainder need not tend to 0. The classic example is f(x) = e^(−1/x²) for x ≠ 0, f(0) = 0: all derivatives at 0 are 0, so the Taylor series is identically 0, but f(x) > 0 for x ≠ 0. To show a Taylor series converges to f you must show Rₙ → 0.

Complex differentiation
f: E → ℂ (E ⊆ ℂ) is differentiable at z if
lim_(h→0, h∈ℂ) (f(z + h) − f(z))/h
exists. The limit must be the same whichever direction h approaches 0 from, which makes this much stronger than real differentiability.
- The sum, product, quotient and chain rules hold with the same proofs, so polynomials are differentiable with d/dz zⁿ = nzⁿ⁻¹.
- f(z) = z̄ is differentiable nowhere: the difference quotient h̄/h equals 1 for real h and −1 for purely imaginary h.
- f(z) = |z|² is differentiable only at 0. The quotient is (zh̄ + z̄h + |h|²)/h = z̄ + z(h̄/h) + h̄, which tends to 0 at z = 0 but has no limit when z ≠ 0.

What does not carry over
Rolle's theorem and the MVT are false for complex-valued functions: f(t) = e^(it) on [0, 2π] has f(0) = f(2π) but f′(t) = ie^(it) is never 0. The real theorems rely on the ordering of ℝ.

Exam tips: in Taylor questions write the remainder explicitly and bound it. In complex differentiation questions, test the difference quotient along the real and imaginary directions to show non-differentiability.

notes.h: Power series and radius of convergence
notes.body:
Power series are how Analysis I defines the exponential and trigonometric functions, so their convergence theory comes first.

Definition
A power series is Σ_(n≥0) aₙzⁿ with aₙ, z ∈ ℂ.

The key lemma
If Σaₙz₁ⁿ converges, then Σaₙzⁿ converges absolutely for every |z| < |z₁|.
Proof: the terms aₙz₁ⁿ tend to 0, so |aₙz₁ⁿ| ≤ K for some K. Then |aₙzⁿ| ≤ K|z/z₁|ⁿ, and Σ|z/z₁|ⁿ is a convergent geometric series since |z/z₁| < 1. Compare.

Radius of convergence
From the lemma there is a unique R ∈ [0, ∞] such that the series converges absolutely for |z| < R and diverges for |z| > R. R is the radius of convergence. On the circle |z| = R anything can happen.

Computing R
- Ratio method: if |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| → l then R = 1/l (with R = ∞ if l = 0, and R = 0 if the ratio → ∞).
- Root method (a standard extra): if |aₙ|^(1/n) → l then R = 1/l.
- In general (the Cauchy–Hadamard formula, a standard extra not named in the schedule) 1/R = lim sup |aₙ|^(1/n).
- Or directly: find when the terms are bounded or tend to 0.

Examples
- Σzⁿ: R = 1; diverges at every point of |z| = 1 (terms do not tend to 0).
- Σzⁿ/n: R = 1; diverges at z = 1 (harmonic series), converges at z = −1 (alternating series test).
- Σzⁿ/n²: R = 1; converges absolutely at every point of |z| = 1 (comparison with Σ1/n²).
- Σzⁿ/n!: R = ∞, since the ratio is 1/(n + 1) → 0.
- Σn! zⁿ: R = 0; converges only at z = 0.
These first three show that the boundary behaviour can be anything.

Worked examples
- Σ(2ⁿ/n)zⁿ: |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = 2n/(n + 1) → 2, so R = 1/2.
- Σn²zⁿ/3ⁿ: ratio (n + 1)²/(3n²) → 1/3, so R = 3.
- Σz^(2n)/4ⁿ = Σ(z²/4)ⁿ: a geometric series in z²/4, converging if and only if |z|² < 4, so R = 2. (Here half the coefficients are zero, so the ratio test cannot be applied to aₙ directly; substitute w = z² first.)

Differentiation term by term
If Σaₙzⁿ has radius R, then the derived series Σnaₙzⁿ⁻¹ also has radius R, and f(z) = Σaₙzⁿ is complex differentiable on |z| < R with
f′(z) = Σ_(n≥1) naₙzⁿ⁻¹.
Hence f has derivatives of all orders inside the disc, and aₙ = f^(n)(0)/n!. The schedule marks the direct proof of this result as non-examinable (starred), but the statement is used constantly.

Uniqueness
If Σaₙzⁿ = Σbₙzⁿ on some disc |z| < r with r > 0, then aₙ = bₙ for all n (differentiate repeatedly and set z = 0). This justifies comparing coefficients.

Exam tips: always state R first, then examine the boundary separately if asked. Watch for series with missing powers (only even powers, or z^(n²)); substitute or use the root test rather than the ratio test.

In Analysis I the familiar functions are defined from power series and their properties are proved, rather than assumed.

The exponential
exp z = Σ_(n≥0) zⁿ/n!, with radius of convergence ∞. By term-by-term differentiation, exp is differentiable on ℂ with exp′ = exp, and exp 0 = 1.

The addition formula
exp(a + b) = exp a · exp b. For real arguments: let F(x) = exp(x) exp(c − x). Then F′(x) = exp(x)exp(c − x) − exp(x)exp(c − x) = 0, so F is constant by the MVT, equal to F(0) = exp c. Taking c = a + b and x = a gives the formula. (For complex arguments one can use the analogous fact that a function on ℂ with zero derivative is constant, or multiply the absolutely convergent series.)

Real exponential and logarithm
For real x:
- exp x > 0: for x ≥ 0 every term is non-negative and exp x ≥ 1; for x < 0, exp x = 1/exp(−x).
- exp is strictly increasing (exp′ = exp > 0) and exp x ≥ 1 + x for x ≥ 0, so exp x → ∞ as x → ∞ and exp x → 0 as x → −∞.
- Hence exp: ℝ → (0, ∞) is a bijection, and its inverse log: (0, ∞) → ℝ is differentiable with log′(y) = 1/y (inverse function rule).
- log(xy) = log x + log y follows from the addition formula.
- Real powers are defined by x^α = exp(α log x) for x > 0, which agrees with the elementary definition for rational α. Then d/dx x^α = αx^(α−1).
- e = exp 1, and eˣ = exp x.

Trigonometric functions
Define for z ∈ ℂ:
cos z = (e^(iz) + e^(−iz))/2 = Σ (−1)ⁿ z^(2n)/(2n)!,
sin z = (e^(iz) − e^(−iz))/(2i) = Σ (−1)ⁿ z^(2n+1)/(2n + 1)!.
Consequences, each a short calculation:
- e^(iz) = cos z + i sin z.
- cos² z + sin² z = 1.
- cos′ = −sin and sin′ = cos.
- addition formulae for cos(z + w) and sin(z + w), from the exponential addition formula.

Defining π
For real x, cos 0 = 1, and the series gives cos 2 < 1 − 2 + 2/3 = −1/3 < 0 (the remaining terms pair into negative amounts). By the IVT cos has a zero in (0, 2); sin > 0 on (0, 2) makes cos strictly decreasing there, so the zero is unique. Define π/2 to be this zero. Then:
- sin(π/2) = 1 and e^(iπ/2) = i, so e^(2πi) = 1;
- exp(z + 2πi) = exp z, so exp is periodic with period 2πi, and cos, sin have period 2π.

Hyperbolic functions
cosh z = (e^z + e^(−z))/2 and sinh z = (e^z − e^(−z))/2. They are related to the trigonometric functions by
cosh z = cos(iz) and sinh z = −i sin(iz),
and satisfy cosh² z − sinh² z = 1, cosh′ = sinh, sinh′ = cosh.

Worked example
Solve cos z = 2 in ℂ. Put w = e^(iz): w + 1/w = 4, so w² − 4w + 1 = 0 and w = 2 ± √3. Then iz = log(2 ± √3) + 2nπi, so z = 2nπ − i log(2 ± √3). Since (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 1, the solutions are z = 2nπ ± i log(2 + √3), n ∈ ℤ. This shows cos is unbounded on ℂ, unlike on ℝ.

Exam tips: proofs of exp(a + b) = exp a exp b and the definition of π are standard bookwork. Be clear about which facts are proved for real arguments and which for complex ones.

Integration has six lectures in the schedule, as many as limits and convergence. The integral is defined by squeezing between upper and lower sums, not as an antiderivative.

Dissections and sums
Let f: [a, b] → ℝ be bounded. A dissection D is a finite set of points a = x₀ < x₁ < ⋯ < xₙ = b. Define
- the upper sum S(f, D) = Σ (xⱼ − xⱼ₋₁) sup_[xⱼ₋₁, xⱼ] f,
- the lower sum s(f, D) = Σ (xⱼ − xⱼ₋₁) inf_[xⱼ₋₁, xⱼ] f.
Key lemmas:
- Refining D (adding points) can only decrease S and increase s.
- For any two dissections D₁, D₂: s(f, D₁) ≤ S(f, D₂) (compare both with D₁ ∪ D₂).
So the upper integral I* = inf_D S(f, D) and lower integral I_* = sup_D s(f, D) satisfy I_* ≤ I*.

Definition
f is Riemann integrable if I_* = I*, and then ∫_a^b f is this common value.

Riemann's criterion
f is integrable if and only if for every ε > 0 there is a dissection D with S(f, D) − s(f, D) < ε. This is the practical test.

A non-integrable function
f = 1 on rationals and 0 on irrationals in [0, 1]. Every subinterval contains both, so every upper sum is 1 and every lower sum is 0. Hence I* = 1 ≠ 0 = I_*.

Monotonic functions are integrable
If f is increasing on [a, b], take n equal pieces of width h = (b − a)/n. On each piece sup f = f(xⱼ) and inf f = f(xⱼ₋₁), so
S − s = h Σ (f(xⱼ) − f(xⱼ₋₁)) = (b − a)(f(b) − f(a))/n,
which is < ε for large n.

Continuous functions are integrable
The schedule lists piecewise-continuous functions; the usual proof for a continuous function uses uniform continuity (the term itself is developed further in Analysis II). A continuous function on [a, b] is uniformly continuous: for every ε there is δ such that |x − y| < δ implies |f(x) − f(y)| < ε, with δ independent of x and y (proof by Bolzano–Weierstrass). Using a dissection with mesh < δ gives S − s ≤ ε(b − a). Piecewise continuous functions are integrable by treating each piece separately.

Worked example
∫_0^1 x dx with n equal pieces: S = Σ_(j=1)^n (1/n)(j/n) = (n + 1)/(2n) and s = Σ_(j=1)^n (1/n)((j − 1)/n) = (n − 1)/(2n). So S − s = 1/n → 0, and both tend to 1/2, so the integral is 1/2.

Properties
For integrable f, g on [a, b]:
- Linearity: ∫(λf + μg) = λ∫f + μ∫g.
- Monotonicity: f ≤ g implies ∫f ≤ ∫g.
- |f| is integrable and |∫f| ≤ ∫|f|.
- fg is integrable.
- Additivity: ∫_a^b = ∫_a^c + ∫_c^b for a < c < b.
- If m ≤ f ≤ M then m(b − a) ≤ ∫_a^b f ≤ M(b − a).

Exam tips: the standard bookwork is 'monotonic implies integrable' and the non-integrable example. Write sums carefully with the correct sup and inf on each subinterval, and always state Riemann's criterion when you use it.

notes.h: The fundamental theorem of calculus and improper integrals
notes.body:
The final section connects integration with differentiation and extends the integral to unbounded intervals and functions.

The fundamental theorem of calculus (FTC)
Part 1: let f be integrable on [a, b] and define F(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt. Then F is continuous, and if f is continuous at x, F is differentiable at x with F′(x) = f(x).
Proof idea: (F(x + h) − F(x))/h − f(x) = (1/h)∫_x^(x+h) (f(t) − f(x)) dt, which is at most sup over |t − x| ≤ |h| of |f(t) − f(x)| in absolute value, and this tends to 0 by continuity.
Part 2: if g is differentiable on [a, b] and g′ is integrable (e.g. continuous), then ∫_a^b g′(t) dt = g(b) − g(a).
Proof idea: for any dissection, the MVT gives g(xⱼ) − g(xⱼ₋₁) = g′(cⱼ)(xⱼ − xⱼ₋₁), which lies between the inf and sup terms. Summing, s ≤ g(b) − g(a) ≤ S for every dissection.

Integration by parts and substitution
- If f, g have continuous derivatives on [a, b]: ∫_a^b f g′ = [fg]_a^b − ∫_a^b f′g. (Apply the FTC to (fg)′ = f′g + fg′.)
- Substitution: if g has a continuous derivative and f is continuous, ∫_g(a)^g(b) f(u) du = ∫_a^b f(g(t)) g′(t) dt.

Taylor's theorem with integral remainder
If f has a continuous nth derivative on an interval containing a and a + h,
f(a + h) = Σ_(k=0)^(n−1) hᵏ f^(k)(a)/k! + Rₙ, where
Rₙ = ∫_a^(a+h) ((a + h − t)^(n−1)/(n − 1)!) f^(n)(t) dt = (hⁿ/(n − 1)!) ∫_0^1 (1 − s)^(n−1) f^(n)(a + sh) ds.
It is proved by repeated integration by parts, starting from f(a + h) − f(a) = ∫_a^(a+h) f′(t) dt.

Improper integrals
- If f is integrable on [a, R] for every R > a, then ∫_a^∞ f = lim_(R→∞) ∫_a^R f, when the limit exists.
- If f is unbounded near a but integrable on [a + δ, b] for each δ > 0, then ∫_a^b f = lim_(δ→0+) ∫_(a+δ)^b f.
Standard examples:
- ∫_1^∞ x^(−k) dx converges if and only if k > 1, and then equals 1/(k − 1).
- ∫_0^1 x^(−k) dx converges if and only if k < 1, and then equals 1/(1 − k).
- ∫_0^∞ e^(−x) dx = lim (1 − e^(−R)) = 1.
- ∫_(−∞)^∞ x dx is not defined: the two halves must converge separately, even though ∫_(−R)^R x dx = 0 for every R.

The integral test (a standard extra, not named in the schedule)
If f is positive and decreasing on [1, ∞), then Σ f(n) and ∫_1^∞ f converge or diverge together. Indeed f(n + 1) ≤ ∫_n^(n+1) f ≤ f(n). Examples:
- Σ 1/nᵏ converges if and only if k > 1.
- Σ 1/(n log n) diverges, since ∫_2^R dx/(x log x) = log log R − log log 2 → ∞.
- The difference Σ_(k=1)^n 1/k − log n decreases to a finite limit (Euler's constant γ ≈ 0.577).

Exam tips: in FTC questions be precise about the hypotheses (continuity of f at x for Part 1; integrability of g′ for Part 2). For improper integrals, write the limit explicitly and evaluate it.

cards.b: For every ε > 0 there exists N such that |aₙ − a| < ε for all n ≥ N.
Every increasing sequence of reals that is bounded above converges (equivalently: every non-empty set bounded above has a supremum).
Every bounded sequence in ℝ (or ℂ) has a convergent subsequence.
For every ε > 0 there exists N with |aₘ − aₙ| < ε for all m, n ≥ N.
A sequence in ℝ or ℂ converges if and only if it is Cauchy.
Take ε = 1: for n ≥ N, |aₙ| < |a| + 1; so |aₙ| ≤ max(|a₁|, …, |a_(N−1)|, |a| + 1) for all n.

cards.f: Does the fundamental axiom hold in ℚ?
cards.b: No: the decimal truncations of √2 form an increasing bounded sequence of rationals with no rational limit.

cards.f: Necessary condition for Σaₙ to converge
cards.b: aₙ → 0. Not sufficient: Σ1/n diverges although 1/n → 0.
Σ_(n≥0) xⁿ converges if and only if |x| < 1, and then equals 1/(1 − x).
Converges if and only if k > 1 (k = 1 is the divergent harmonic series).
If 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ and Σbₙ converges then Σaₙ converges (partial sums increase and are bounded).
If |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| → l: l < 1 gives absolute convergence, l > 1 divergence, l = 1 no conclusion.
If aₙ decreases to 0 then Σ(−1)^(n+1) aₙ converges.

cards.f: Absolute convergence implies convergence: key inequality
cards.b: |aₘ₊₁ + ⋯ + aₙ| ≤ |aₘ₊₁| + ⋯ + |aₙ|, so Cauchy partial sums of Σ|aₙ| give Cauchy partial sums of Σaₙ.
Σ(−1)^(n+1)/n converges (alternating series test) but Σ1/n diverges.
For every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that x ∈ E and |x − a| < δ imply |f(x) − f(a)| < ε.
f is continuous at a if and only if f(xₙ) → f(a) for every sequence xₙ in E with xₙ → a.
If f: [a, b] → ℝ is continuous and η lies strictly between f(a) and f(b), then f(c) = η for some c ∈ (a, b).
A continuous f: [a, b] → ℝ is bounded and attains its supremum and infimum.

cards.f: Set used in the IVT proof
cards.b: S = {x ∈ [a, b] : f(x) < η}, with c = sup S; continuity rules out f(c) < η and f(c) > η.
f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1): the interval is not closed, so the boundedness theorem does not apply.

cards.f: Is x sin(1/x) (with f(0) = 0) continuous at 0?
cards.b: Yes: |f(x) − f(0)| ≤ |x|, so take δ = ε.
f′(x) = lim_(h→0) (f(x + h) − f(x))/h; equivalently f(x + h) = f(x) + hf′(x) + hε(h) with ε(h) → 0.
f continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), f(a) = f(b) ⇒ f′(c) = 0 for some c ∈ (a, b).
f continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b) ⇒ f(b) − f(a) = f′(c)(b − a) for some c ∈ (a, b).
g(x) = f(x) − kx with k = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a), so g(a) = g(b); then apply Rolle.
(f(b) − f(a))g′(c) = (g(b) − g(a))f′(c) for some c ∈ (a, b), under the MVT hypotheses on f and g.
If f′ > 0 and g = f⁻¹ then g′(y) = 1/f′(g(y)).
x² sin(1/x) (0 at 0): f′(0) = 0 but f′(x) = 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x) has no limit at 0.
Yes: f(x + h) − f(x) = h(f′(x) + ε(h)) → 0. The converse fails, e.g. |x| at 0.
f(a + h) = Σ_(k=0)^(n−1) hᵏf^(k)(a)/k! + (hⁿ/n!) f^(n)(a + θh) for some θ ∈ (0, 1).
Is the mean value theorem: f(a + h) = f(a) + hf′(a + θh).
≤ |x|⁵/120, from Taylor with n = 5 since the fifth derivative is cos, bounded by 1.

cards.f: Smooth function whose Taylor series at 0 does not converge to it
cards.b: f(x) = e^(−1/x²) (x ≠ 0), f(0) = 0: all derivatives vanish at 0, but f(x) > 0 for x ≠ 0.
f′(z) = lim (f(z + h) − f(z))/h as h → 0 through ℂ; the limit must not depend on the direction of approach.
Nowhere: the quotient h̄/h is 1 for real h and −1 for imaginary h.
Only at z = 0; elsewhere the quotient z̄ + z h̄/h + h̄ has no limit.

cards.f: Does Rolle's theorem hold for complex-valued f?
cards.b: No: e^(it) on [0, 2π] takes equal values at the ends but its derivative ie^(it) never vanishes.
The unique R ∈ [0, ∞] with Σaₙzⁿ absolutely convergent for |z| < R and divergent for |z| > R.
If Σaₙz₁ⁿ converges then Σaₙzⁿ converges absolutely whenever |z| < |z₁| (compare with a geometric series).
If |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| → l then R = 1/l (R = ∞ when l = 0).
1/R = lim sup |aₙ|^(1/n).
Σzⁿ diverges everywhere on |z| = 1; Σzⁿ/n diverges at 1 but converges at −1; Σzⁿ/n² converges everywhere on |z| = 1.
Inside its radius R, f(z) = Σaₙzⁿ is differentiable with f′(z) = Σnaₙzⁿ⁻¹, a series with the same radius R.
∞: the ratio of successive coefficients is 1/(n + 1) → 0.
exp z = Σ_(n≥0) zⁿ/n!, convergent for all z ∈ ℂ, with exp′ = exp and exp 0 = 1.

cards.f: Proof idea for exp(a + b) = exp a exp b (real case)
cards.b: F(x) = exp(x)exp(c − x) has F′ = 0, so F is constant = exp c; set c = a + b, x = a.
log′(y) = 1/y, by the inverse function rule since exp′ = exp.
x^α = exp(α log x) for x > 0; then d/dx x^α = αx^(α−1).

cards.f: cos z and sin z via exp
cards.b: cos z = (e^(iz) + e^(−iz))/2 and sin z = (e^(iz) − e^(−iz))/(2i).

cards.f: Definition of π in Analysis I
cards.b: π/2 is the unique zero of cos in (0, 2): cos 0 = 1 > 0, cos 2 < −1/3 < 0, and cos is strictly decreasing there.

cards.f: cosh and sinh in terms of cos and sin
cards.b: cosh z = cos(iz) and sinh z = −i sin(iz).
2πi: e^(2πi) = 1, so exp(z + 2πi) = exp z.
Σ (xⱼ − xⱼ₋₁) × sup of f on [xⱼ₋₁, xⱼ], over the dissection a = x₀ < ⋯ < xₙ = b.
f bounded on [a, b] with sup over D of lower sums = inf over D of upper sums; the common value is ∫_a^b f.
f is integrable if and only if for every ε > 0 there is a dissection D with S(f, D) − s(f, D) < ε.
f = 1 on ℚ, 0 elsewhere, on [0, 1]: every upper sum is 1 and every lower sum is 0.

cards.f: S − s for increasing f with n equal pieces
cards.b: (b − a)(f(b) − f(a))/n, which tends to 0, so monotonic functions are integrable.
Upper sums can only decrease and lower sums only increase; hence every lower sum ≤ every upper sum.
Continuity on [a, b] is uniform, so a fine enough dissection makes sup − inf < ε on each piece, giving S − s ≤ ε(b − a).
|∫_a^b f| ≤ ∫_a^b |f| for integrable f (|f| is integrable too).
If f is integrable and continuous at x, then F(x) = ∫_a^x f has F′(x) = f(x).
If g is differentiable on [a, b] with g′ integrable, then ∫_a^b g′ = g(b) − g(a).
∫_a^b f g′ = [fg]_a^b − ∫_a^b f′g, for f, g with continuous derivatives.

cards.f: Integral form of the Taylor remainder

cards.b: Converges if and only if k > 1, with value 1/(k − 1).
Converges if and only if k < 1, with value 1/(1 − k).
For f positive and decreasing, Σf(n) and ∫_1^∞ f converge or diverge together, since f(n + 1) ≤ ∫_n^(n+1) f ≤ f(n).
No: ∫_2^R dx/(x log x) = log log R − log log 2 → ∞, so by the integral test it diverges.

questions.q: For aₙ = (2n + 1)/(n + 3), which choice of N guarantees |aₙ − 2| < ε for all n ≥ N?
options: No N works because aₙ never equals 2
questions.why: |aₙ − 2| = 5/(n + 3) < 5/n, which is < ε once n > 5/ε. N > 1/ε is not enough for small ε (e.g. ε = 0.1, n = 11 gives 5/14 > 0.1). A fixed N cannot work for all ε. Convergence does not require any term to equal the limit.

questions.q: Which statement is FALSE?
options: Every Cauchy sequence of reals converges
Every bounded monotone real sequence converges
questions.why: (−1)ⁿ is bounded but does not converge; Bolzano–Weierstrass only gives a convergent subsequence. The other three are standard theorems: the general principle of convergence, boundedness of convergent sequences, and the monotone (fundamental axiom) result.

questions.q: Prove that a Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges. You may assume the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem.
markScheme: Shows a Cauchy sequence is bounded (ε = 1)
Applies Bolzano–Weierstrass to get a subsequence a_(nⱼ) → a
Given ε, chooses N from the Cauchy condition with ε/2 and J with |a_(nⱼ) − a| < ε/2
Triangle inequality |aₘ − a| ≤ |aₘ − a_(nⱼ)| + |a_(nⱼ) − a| < ε for m ≥ N
Concludes aₘ → a
questions.modelAnswer: Let (aₙ) be Cauchy. With ε = 1 there is N₁ such that |aₘ − a_(N₁)| < 1 for m ≥ N₁, so |aₘ| ≤ max(|a₁|, …, |a_(N₁)|) + 1 for all m: the sequence is bounded. By Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a subsequence a_(nⱼ) → a. Let ε > 0. Choose N with |aₘ − aₙ| < ε/2 for all m, n ≥ N, and choose j with nⱼ ≥ N and |a_(nⱼ) − a| < ε/2 (possible since nⱼ → ∞ and a_(nⱼ) → a). Then for m ≥ N, |aₘ − a| ≤ |aₘ − a_(nⱼ)| + |a_(nⱼ) − a| < ε/2 + ε/2 = ε. So aₘ → a.

questions.q: Which series diverges?
questions.why: Σ 1/√n = Σ 1/n^(1/2) diverges since 1/2 ≤ 1 (compare: 1/√n ≥ 1/n). Σ1/n² converges (k = 2 > 1); Σ(−1)ⁿ/n converges by the alternating series test; Σ n/3ⁿ converges by the ratio test with limit 1/3.

questions.q: Applying the ratio test to Σ n!/nⁿ gives the limit:
questions.why: aₙ₊₁/aₙ = (n + 1)! nⁿ / ((n + 1)^(n+1) n!) = nⁿ/(n + 1)ⁿ = (1 + 1/n)^(−n) → 1/e < 1, so the series converges. Answer 1 comes from the common error that n/(n + 1) → 1 forces (n/(n + 1))ⁿ → 1; the power n matters, and the limit is 1/e. Answer e is the reciprocal, from computing aₙ/aₙ₊₁ instead. Answer 0 comes from wrongly treating nⁿ/(n + 1)ⁿ as vanishing because (n + 1)ⁿ grows faster than nⁿ; their ratio stays near 1/e.

questions.q: Prove that if Σ|aₙ| converges then Σaₙ converges (aₙ ∈ ℂ). Give an example showing the converse is false.
markScheme: Partial sums of Σ|aₙ| converge, hence are Cauchy
Triangle inequality bounds |sₙ − sₘ| by tₙ − tₘ
So (sₙ) is Cauchy and converges by the general principle
Counterexample Σ(−1)^(n+1)/n with justification of convergence (alternating series test)
and divergence of Σ1/n
questions.modelAnswer: Let sₙ = a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ and tₙ = |a₁| + ⋯ + |aₙ|. Since (tₙ) converges it is Cauchy: given ε > 0 there is N with |tₙ − tₘ| < ε for n > m ≥ N. Then |sₙ − sₘ| = |aₘ₊₁ + ⋯ + aₙ| ≤ |aₘ₊₁| + ⋯ + |aₙ| = tₙ − tₘ < ε. So (sₙ) is Cauchy and converges by the general principle of convergence. The converse fails: Σ(−1)^(n+1)/n converges by the alternating series test, as 1/n decreases to 0, but Σ|(−1)^(n+1)/n| = Σ1/n diverges.

questions.q: Which function on the given domain must attain its maximum?
questions.why: x² − x is continuous on the closed bounded interval [0, 2], so it attains its maximum (2, at x = 2). On (0, 1) the identity approaches 1 but never reaches it; 1/x is unbounded on (0, 1]; the function equal to x on [0, 1) with f(1) = 0 is discontinuous at 1 and never reaches its supremum 1.

questions.q: Which statement follows from the intermediate value theorem?
options: Every polynomial with real coefficients has a real root
Every continuous function on ℝ is bounded
A continuous f: (0, 1) → (0, 1) has a fixed point
questions.why: p(0) = 1 > 0 and p(1) = 1 − 3 + 1 = −1 < 0, so p has a root in (0, 1). x² + 1 has no real root, so not every real polynomial has a real root. The function x on ℝ is continuous but unbounded, so continuous functions on ℝ need not be bounded. f(x) = x² maps (0, 1) to itself with no fixed point there (the closed interval is needed).

questions.q: Prove that a continuous function f: [a, b] → ℝ is bounded. Where does your proof use that the interval is closed?
markScheme: Assumes for contradiction there are xₙ with |f(xₙ)| > n
Bolzano–Weierstrass gives a convergent subsequence x_(nⱼ) → x
x ∈ [a, b] because a ≤ x_(nⱼ) ≤ b and limits preserve non-strict inequalities
Continuity gives f(x_(nⱼ)) → f(x), so the subsequence of values is bounded: contradiction
Identifies the closedness step explicitly
questions.modelAnswer: Suppose f is unbounded. Then for each n there is xₙ ∈ [a, b] with |f(xₙ)| > n. The sequence (xₙ) is bounded, so by Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a convergent subsequence x_(nⱼ) → x. Since a ≤ x_(nⱼ) ≤ b and non-strict inequalities pass to limits, x ∈ [a, b]. This is where closedness is used: on (0, 1], for instance, the limit could be 0, outside the domain. As f is continuous at x, f(x_(nⱼ)) → f(x), so (f(x_(nⱼ))) is bounded. But |f(x_(nⱼ))| > nⱼ ≥ j for every j, a contradiction. Hence f is bounded.

questions.q: For f(x) = x³ on [0, 3], which c satisfies the conclusion of the mean value theorem?
questions.why: (f(3) − f(0))/3 = 27/3 = 9, and f′(c) = 3c² = 9 gives c = √3 ∈ (0, 3). c = 3/2 is the midpoint (f′ = 6.75); c = 1 gives f′ = 3; 9 is the value of the slope, not of c, and lies outside the interval.

questions.q: Rolle's theorem does NOT apply to f(x) = |x| on [−1, 1] because:
questions.why: |x| is continuous with f(−1) = f(1) = 1 on a closed interval, but it is not differentiable at 0 ∈ (−1, 1); indeed no c has f′(c) = 0. The other options are false statements about this function.

questions.q: State the mean value theorem and use it to prove that if f′(x) > 0 for all x in an interval I then f is strictly increasing on I. Deduce that x/(1 + x) < log(1 + x) for x > 0.
markScheme: Correct statement of the MVT with hypotheses
For x < y in I, f(y) − f(x) = f′(c)(y − x) > 0
Sets g(x) = log(1 + x) − x/(1 + x), g(0) = 0
Concludes g(x) > g(0) = 0 for x > 0
questions.modelAnswer: MVT: if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), there is c ∈ (a, b) with f(b) − f(a) = f′(c)(b − a). If f′ > 0 on I and x < y in I, f is differentiable (hence continuous) on [x, y], so f(y) − f(x) = f′(c)(y − x) for some c ∈ (x, y), and this is positive. So f is strictly increasing. Now let g(x) = log(1 + x) − x/(1 + x) for x ≥ 0. Then g′(x) = 1/(1 + x) − [(1 + x) − x]/(1 + x)² = 1/(1 + x) − 1/(1 + x)² = x/(1 + x)², which is > 0 for x > 0. Applying the result on [0, ∞) (or the MVT on [0, x]), g(x) > g(0) = 0, i.e. log(1 + x) > x/(1 + x) for x > 0.

questions.q: The Taylor expansion of log(1 + x) about 0 to second order is x − x²/2 + R₃. Which is the Lagrange form of R₃?
questions.why: f‴(t) = 2/(1 + t)³, so R₃ = (x³/3!) · 2/(1 + θx)³ = x³/(3(1 + θx)³). x³/(6(1 + θx)³) forgets the factor 2 in f‴; −x³/(3(1 + θx)³) has the wrong sign, since f‴ > 0; x³/3 is the next Taylor term, not the exact remainder.

questions.q: Which function is complex differentiable at every point of ℂ?
questions.why: Polynomials in z are differentiable everywhere, with f′(z) = 3z² − 2. z̄ and Re z give different difference quotients along real and imaginary directions; |z| is complex differentiable nowhere: at 0 the quotient |h|/h depends on the direction of h, and at z ≠ 0 the quotient tends to Re z/|z| (a real number) along real h and to −i Im z/|z| (an imaginary number) along imaginary h, and these agree only if Re z = Im z = 0.

questions.q: Use Taylor's theorem to show that |cos x − 1 + x²/2| ≤ x⁴/24 for all real x. Hence find lim_(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x².
markScheme: Derivatives of cos at 0: 1, 0, −1, 0, fourth derivative cos
Taylor with n = 4: cos x = 1 − x²/2 + (x⁴/24) cos(θx)
Bounds the remainder by x⁴/24 using |cos| ≤ 1
Writes (1 − cos x)/x² = 1/2 − (x²/24) cos(θx)
Concludes the limit is 1/2
questions.modelAnswer: Let f = cos. Then f(0) = 1, f′(0) = −sin 0 = 0, f″(0) = −cos 0 = −1, f‴(0) = sin 0 = 0 and f⁗ = cos. Taylor's theorem with n = 4 at a = 0 gives cos x = 1 + 0·x − x²/2 + 0·x³ + (x⁴/24) cos(θx) for some θ ∈ (0, 1). Since |cos(θx)| ≤ 1, |cos x − 1 + x²/2| ≤ x⁴/24. Then for x ≠ 0, (1 − cos x)/x² = 1/2 − (x²/24)cos(θx), and |(1 − cos x)/x² − 1/2| ≤ x²/24 → 0. So the limit is 1/2.

questions.q: What is the radius of convergence of Σ (2ⁿ/n) zⁿ?
questions.why: |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = 2ⁿ⁺¹n/((n + 1)2ⁿ) = 2n/(n + 1) → 2, so R = 1/2. Answer 2 inverts the formula; the factor 1/n does not affect R, so 1 is wrong; R = ∞ would need the ratio to tend to 0.

questions.q: The power series Σ zⁿ/n has radius 1. At which point on |z| = 1 does it diverge?
options: It diverges at every point of |z| = 1
questions.why: At z = 1 it is the harmonic series, which diverges. At z = −1 it is an alternating series with terms decreasing to 0, so it converges; at other points of the circle (including i) it also converges, though that needs a finer argument. So it does not diverge everywhere on the circle.

questions.q: Find the radius of convergence of Σ (n!/nⁿ) zⁿ.
markScheme: Writes aₙ₊₁/aₙ correctly
Simplifies to (n/(n + 1))ⁿ = (1 + 1/n)^(−n)
Uses (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e
Limit of the ratio is 1/e
Concludes R = e
questions.modelAnswer: With aₙ = n!/nⁿ, aₙ₊₁/aₙ = (n + 1)!/(n + 1)^(n+1) × nⁿ/n! = (n + 1)nⁿ/(n + 1)^(n+1) = nⁿ/(n + 1)ⁿ = (1 + 1/n)^(−n). Since (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e, the ratio tends to 1/e. By the ratio method the radius of convergence is R = 1/(1/e) = e.

questions.q: Which identity is correct for all z ∈ ℂ?
questions.why: cos(iz) = (e^(−z) + e^z)/2 = cosh z. In fact sin(iz) = i sinh z, so sinh z = −i sin(iz), not i sin(iz). cosh(iz) = cos z, not cosh z in general. The Pythagorean identity is cos² z + sin² z = 1.

questions.q: In Analysis I, why does cos have a zero in (0, 2)?
options: Because cos is periodic with period 2π
Because cos 0 = 1 and cos 2 < 0, so the IVT applies
Because the series for cos has only even powers
questions.why: From the series, cos 2 < 1 − 2 + 2/3 = −1/3, and cos is continuous, so the IVT gives a zero in (0, 2). Periodicity with period 2π is derived after π is defined, so using it is circular. sin 2 ≠ 0. Even powers make cos an even function but do not give a zero.

questions.q: Solve cos z = 2 for z ∈ ℂ.
markScheme: Substitutes w = e^(iz) to get w + 1/w = 4
Solves w² − 4w + 1 = 0, w = 2 ± √3
Takes logarithms: iz = log(2 ± √3) + 2nπi
Uses (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 1 to simplify
z = 2nπ ± i log(2 + √3), n ∈ ℤ
questions.modelAnswer: cos z = (e^(iz) + e^(−iz))/2 = 2. Let w = e^(iz) ≠ 0. Then w + 1/w = 4, so w² − 4w + 1 = 0 and w = 2 ± √3, both positive reals. e^(iz) = w means iz = log w + 2nπi for n ∈ ℤ (as exp has period 2πi), so z = 2nπ − i log(2 ± √3). Since (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1, log(2 − √3) = −log(2 + √3). Hence the solutions are z = 2nπ ± i log(2 + √3), n ∈ ℤ.

questions.q: Which function is NOT Riemann integrable on [0, 1]?
options: f(x) = 1 if x is rational, else 0
questions.why: The indicator of ℚ has all upper sums 1 and lower sums 0. Changing a function at one point does not affect integrability; ⌊10x⌋ is monotonic (piecewise constant); x sin(1/x) with f(0) = 0 is continuous on [0, 1].

questions.q: Prove that an increasing function f: [a, b] → ℝ is Riemann integrable.
markScheme: f is bounded by f(a) and f(b)
Takes the dissection with n equal pieces of width (b − a)/n
Identifies sup = f(xⱼ), inf = f(xⱼ₋₁) on each piece
Telescopes: S − s = (b − a)(f(b) − f(a))/n
Chooses n large and applies Riemann's criterion
questions.modelAnswer: Since f is increasing, f(a) ≤ f(x) ≤ f(b), so f is bounded. Let ε > 0 and take Dₙ with xⱼ = a + j(b − a)/n. On [xⱼ₋₁, xⱼ] the supremum of f is f(xⱼ) and the infimum is f(xⱼ₋₁). So S(f, Dₙ) − s(f, Dₙ) = Σ_(j=1)^n ((b − a)/n)(f(xⱼ) − f(xⱼ₋₁)) = ((b − a)/n)(f(b) − f(a)), the sum telescoping. Choose n > (b − a)(f(b) − f(a))/ε; then S − s < ε. By Riemann's criterion f is integrable.

questions.q: Let F(x) = ∫_0^(x²) sin(t²) dt. What is F′(x)?
questions.why: Write F = G ∘ u with G(y) = ∫_0^y sin(t²) dt and u(x) = x². By the FTC, G′(y) = sin(y²); by the chain rule F′(x) = sin(x⁴)·2x. sin(x²) substitutes x instead of x² and drops the chain-rule factor, sin(x⁴) forgets u′(x) = 2x, and 2x cos(x⁴) replaces sin by cos, as if the integrand had been differentiated rather than evaluated at the upper limit.

questions.q: Which improper integral converges?
questions.why: ∫_1^∞ x^(−3/2) dx converges (k = 3/2 > 1) with value 1/(1/2) = 2. ∫_1^∞ 1/x diverges (log R → ∞); ∫_0^1 x^(−2) diverges (needs k < 1); ∫_0^∞ 1 dx = lim R = ∞.

questions.q: Let f: [a, b] → ℝ be integrable and continuous at x ∈ (a, b), and let F(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt. Prove that F′(x) = f(x).
markScheme: Writes F(x + h) − F(x) = ∫_x^(x+h) f(t) dt (additivity)
Writes the difference quotient minus f(x) as (1/h)∫_x^(x+h) (f(t) − f(x)) dt
Uses continuity: given ε, δ with |f(t) − f(x)| < ε for |t − x| < δ
Bounds the integral by ε|h| so the quotient differs from f(x) by at most ε
Concludes the limit is f(x) (handles h < 0 too)
questions.modelAnswer: For small h ≠ 0 with x + h ∈ [a, b], additivity gives F(x + h) − F(x) = ∫_x^(x+h) f(t) dt (interpreted as −∫_(x+h)^x when h < 0). Since ∫_x^(x+h) f(x) dt = hf(x), we get (F(x + h) − F(x))/h − f(x) = (1/h)∫_x^(x+h) (f(t) − f(x)) dt. Given ε > 0, continuity at x gives δ > 0 with |f(t) − f(x)| < ε whenever |t − x| < δ. For 0 < |h| < δ every t between x and x + h satisfies this, so |∫_x^(x+h) (f(t) − f(x)) dt| ≤ ε|h|. Hence |(F(x + h) − F(x))/h − f(x)| ≤ ε for 0 < |h| < δ, so F′(x) = f(x).

questions.q:
(a) State and prove the intermediate value theorem for a continuous function f: [a, b] → ℝ. [7]
(b) Prove that a continuous function f: [a, b] → ℝ is bounded and attains its supremum. You may use the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem. [8]
(c) Show that every continuous f: [0, 1] → [0, 1] has a fixed point. Give, with justification, a continuous g: (0, 1) → (0, 1) with no fixed point. [5]
markScheme: (a) Correct statement; defines S = {x : f(x) < η} and c = sup S
(a) Rules out f(c) < η (points to the right of c in S) and f(c) > η (a smaller upper bound) using continuity
(b) Boundedness: unbounded ⇒ |f(xₙ)| > n; BW subsequence converges in [a, b]; continuity contradiction
(b) Attainment: if f < M = sup f everywhere, 1/(M − f) is continuous hence bounded, contradicting sup
(c) h(x) = f(x) − x has h(0) ≥ 0, h(1) ≤ 0; IVT (or endpoint case) gives a root
(c) Example g(x) = x² (or similar) with check that g(x) = x has no solution in (0, 1)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) IVT: if f: [a, b] → ℝ is continuous and f(a) < η < f(b), then there is c ∈ (a, b) with f(c) = η. Proof: S = {x ∈ [a, b] : f(x) < η} contains a and is bounded above by b, so c = sup S exists and a ≤ c ≤ b. Suppose f(c) < η. Then c ≠ b (as f(b) > η), and by continuity there is δ > 0 with f(x) < η for x ∈ [c, c + δ) ∩ [a, b]; such x > c lie in S, contradicting c = sup S. Suppose f(c) > η. Then c ≠ a, and there is δ > 0 with f(x) > η for x ∈ (c − δ, c] ∩ [a, b]; so no point of S lies in (c − δ, c]; since S also has no points above c, every point of S is at most c − δ, so c − δ is an upper bound for S smaller than c, contradicting that c is the least upper bound. Hence f(c) = η, and c ≠ a, b as f(a) < η < f(b).

(b) Suppose f is unbounded. Choose xₙ ∈ [a, b] with |f(xₙ)| > n. By Bolzano–Weierstrass some subsequence x_(nⱼ) → x, and a ≤ x ≤ b because the interval is closed. By continuity f(x_(nⱼ)) → f(x), so the values are bounded, but |f(x_(nⱼ))| > nⱼ → ∞. Contradiction, so f is bounded. Let M = sup f, which exists by completeness. Suppose f(x) < M for all x. Then g(x) = 1/(M − f(x)) is continuous on [a, b], so bounded by the first part, say g ≤ K with K > 0. Then M − f(x) ≥ 1/K for all x, so f ≤ M − 1/K, contradicting that M is the least upper bound. Hence f(x) = M for some x.

(c) Let h(x) = f(x) − x, continuous on [0, 1]. Since 0 ≤ f ≤ 1, h(0) = f(0) ≥ 0 and h(1) = f(1) − 1 ≤ 0. If h(0) = 0 or h(1) = 0 we have a fixed point; otherwise h(0) > 0 > h(1) and the IVT gives c with h(c) = 0, i.e. f(c) = c. For the open interval, take g(x) = x². It maps (0, 1) into (0, 1) and is continuous, but x² = x gives x = 0 or 1, neither of which is in (0, 1). So g has no fixed point; the argument above fails because the endpoints are missing.

questions.q:
(a) Let Σaₙzⁿ be a complex power series. Prove that if it converges at z = z₁ then it converges absolutely for all |z| < |z₁|. Deduce the existence of a radius of convergence. [7]
(b) Find the radius of convergence of (i) Σ n²zⁿ/3ⁿ and (ii) Σ zⁿ/n². Determine whether series (ii) converges at points with |z| equal to its radius. [6]
(c) Define exp z = Σ zⁿ/n!. Assuming that a power series may be differentiated term by term inside its radius of convergence, prove that exp(a + b) = exp(a) exp(b) for all real a, b, and that exp x > 0 for all real x. [7]
markScheme: (a) Terms aₙz₁ⁿ → 0 hence bounded by K
(a) |aₙzⁿ| ≤ K|z/z₁|ⁿ; comparison with geometric series
(a) R = sup{|z| : series converges} gives absolute convergence inside and divergence outside
(b)(i) ratio (n + 1)²/(3n²) → 1/3 so R = 3
(b)(ii) R = 1; on |z| = 1, |zⁿ/n²| = 1/n² so converges absolutely
(c) R = ∞ (ratio 1/(n + 1) → 0), exp′ = exp
(c) F(x) = exp(x)exp(c − x) has F′ = 0, so constant by MVT; deduce addition formula
(c) Positivity: exp x ≥ 1 for x ≥ 0 and exp(x)exp(−x) = 1
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Since Σaₙz₁ⁿ converges, aₙz₁ⁿ → 0, so there is K with |aₙz₁ⁿ| ≤ K for all n. If |z| < |z₁| then |aₙzⁿ| = |aₙz₁ⁿ| |z/z₁|ⁿ ≤ K rⁿ, where r = |z/z₁| < 1. Σ Krⁿ is a convergent geometric series, so Σ|aₙzⁿ| converges by comparison. Now let R = sup{|z| : Σaₙzⁿ converges} ∈ [0, ∞]. If |z| < R, there is z₁ with |z| < |z₁| ≤ R at which the series converges, so it converges absolutely at z. If |z| > R the series diverges at z by definition of R. So R is a radius of convergence.

(b)(i) aₙ = n²/3ⁿ: aₙ₊₁/aₙ = (n + 1)²/(3n²) → 1/3, so R = 3. (ii) aₙ = 1/n²: aₙ₊₁/aₙ = n²/(n + 1)² → 1, so R = 1. On |z| = 1, |zⁿ/n²| = 1/n² and Σ1/n² converges, so the series converges absolutely at every point of the circle.

(c) For exp, the coefficient ratio is (1/(n + 1)!)/(1/n!) = 1/(n + 1) → 0, so R = ∞. Differentiating term by term, exp′(z) = Σ_(n≥1) nzⁿ⁻¹/n! = Σ_(m≥0) zᵐ/m! = exp z, and exp 0 = 1. Fix real c and let F(x) = exp(x) exp(c − x) for real x. By the product and chain rules F′(x) = exp(x)exp(c − x) − exp(x)exp(c − x) = 0. By the mean value theorem F is constant, so F(x) = F(0) = exp(0)exp(c) = exp c. Given real a, b, take c = a + b and x = a: exp(a)exp(b) = exp(a + b). For positivity: if x ≥ 0 every term xⁿ/n! is non-negative and the first is 1, so exp x ≥ 1 > 0. If x < 0, exp(x)exp(−x) = exp 0 = 1 with exp(−x) ≥ 1 > 0, so exp x = 1/exp(−x) > 0.
